extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly / educated general public interested in scientific debates and the woman question
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for assessing scientific arguments about brain, sex differences, and related physiological claims, aimed at judging whether inferences (e.g., from brain size to mental capacity) are scientifically warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not deduce principles unsupported by facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who profess to hold a commission from Science should be bound to the 'scientific rule of deducing no principle which facts will not prove.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that asserted general laws be corroborated by empirical evidence; be skeptical of sweeping conclusions based on incomplete or imperfect data. Example anti-pattern: invoking 'Science' rhetorically to justify a claim unsupported by facts (e.g., asserting innate mental inferiority of women on inadequate grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring internal structure from external product without internal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: We can never reason from product to structure until we have internal evidence of the functional relations between structure and product for that class of organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conclude details about organ anatomy or mechanism merely from observed outputs. Example: one cannot infer the brain's internal organization solely from measures of intellectual 'product' without anatomical/physiological evidence linking structure to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for environmental/contextual differences in comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons of organ function (or behavioral/productive output) must be made under the same environment; different environments can change absolute product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing groups (e.g., male vs. female brains), eliminate or account for differing 'mental atmospheres' or environments that could affect outputs. Example given: comparing lungs at sea level vs. Mont Blanc — absolute product differs because of environment; analogous confounds apply to brain performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain is exceptional — be cautious using analogies from other organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if other organs work in proportion to their size, the brain's variety and complexity of functions make simple size-to-power analogies (biceps→brain) questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid direct analogical inference that 'larger organ = proportionally larger capacity' when the organ in question (the brain) has unique complexity. Anti-pattern: treating brain size exactly like muscle size when arguing about cognitive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurements alone (e.g., brain weights) are insufficient without understanding structure-function mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Students refuse to draw laws of brain capacity from measurements because the precise connection between brain-structure and thought has not been accurately determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat brain-weight/size statistics as potentially informative but not definitive; they should not be the sole basis for concluding innate cognitive superiority. If measurements are used, explicitly acknowledge limitations and the need for corroborating structural/functional evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controlled comparative experiments as the key method where anatomy is indecisive
rubrics_metrics.description: Where anatomy cannot solve the enigma (e.g., of sexual brain-power), recourse should be had to comparison under similar environment as the key to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experimental or carefully controlled observational comparisons that place subjects of different groups in equivalent conditions, rather than relying on uncontrolled historical product differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss relevant data that are central to your own argument
rubrics_metrics.description: If an argument relies on certain statistics (e.g., brain measurements) as its keystone, the proponent cannot concurrently dismiss those measurements as incomplete evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal consistency: if a dataset is foundational to your logic, you must either defend its use or revise the argument. Anti-pattern: cherry-picking—dismissing measurements when inconvenient but using them when they appear to support your claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate confounding influences acting upon comparison groups before inferring innate differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinkers will not infer capacity differences of male and female brains from products until the different influences acting upon men and women can be eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require identification and control (or at least accounting) of social, educational, cultural, and physiological factors that differentially affect the groups compared before concluding innate superiority/inferiority.
